claim: Around 240 million people worldwide suffer from chronic HBV infection.
source: Despite the availability of a vaccine, around 240 people worldwide suffer from chronic HBV infection (Ott et al., 2012), placing them at risk for severe liver disease, such as cirrhosis and cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ott et al., 2012.

claim: Chronic HBV infection places people at risk for severe liver disease, such as cirrhosis and cancer.
source: Despite the availability of a vaccine, around 240 people worldwide suffer from chronic HBV infection (Ott et al., 2012), placing them at risk for severe liver disease, such as cirrhosis and cancer.
evidence: The claim is supported by established medical knowledge and the citation context.

claim: Disruption of the HBV capsid represents a promising approach for treatment of HBV.
source: Among new strategies being explored for the treatment of HBV, disruption of its capsid represents a promising approach (Zlotnick and Mukhopadhyay, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zlotnick and Mukhopadhyay, 2011.

claim: The HBV capsid typically manifests as a T = 4 icosahedral particle, 36 nm in diameter.
source: The HBV capsid typically manifests as a T = 4 icosahedral particle, 36 nm in diameter, composed of 120 copies of capsid protein (Cp) homodimer.
evidence: The claim is based on established structural knowledge of HBV capsid.

claim: The HBV capsid is composed of 120 copies of capsid protein (Cp) homodimer.
source: The HBV capsid typically manifests as a T = 4 icosahedral particle, 36 nm in diameter, composed of 120 copies of capsid protein (Cp) homodimer.
evidence: The claim is based on established structural knowledge of HBV capsid.

claim: The HBV capsid assembles to enclose the viral genome (pregenomic RNA, pgRNA).
source: The capsid carries out important functional roles throughout the HBV infection cycle, assembling to enclose the viral genome (pregenomic RNA, pgRNA), serving as a container for reverse transcription of single-stranded linear pgRNA to circular double-stranded DNA (ds-DNA), displaying signals for intracellular trafficking and the binding of viral envelope glycoproteins, and dissociating to release its cargo to the host cell nucleus (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The HBV capsid serves as a container for reverse transcription of single-stranded linear pgRNA to circular double-stranded DNA (ds-DNA).
source: The capsid carries out important functional roles throughout the HBV infection cycle, assembling to enclose the viral genome (pregenomic RNA, pgRNA), serving as a container for reverse transcription of single-stranded linear pgRNA to circular double-stranded DNA (ds-DNA), displaying signals for intracellular trafficking and the binding of viral envelope glycoproteins, and dissociating to release its cargo to the host cell nucleus (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The HBV capsid displays signals for intracellular trafficking and the binding of viral envelope glycoproteins.
source: The capsid carries out important functional roles throughout the HBV infection cycle, assembling to enclose the viral genome (pregenomic RNA, pgRNA), serving as a container for reverse transcription of single-stranded linear pgRNA to circular double-stranded DNA (ds-DNA), displaying signals for intracellular trafficking and the binding of viral envelope glycoproteins, and dissociating to release its cargo to the host cell nucleus (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The HBV capsid dissociates to release its cargo to the host cell nucleus.
source: The capsid carries out important functional roles throughout the HBV infection cycle, assembling to enclose the viral genome (pregenomic RNA, pgRNA), serving as a container for reverse transcription of single-stranded linear pgRNA to circular double-stranded DNA (ds-DNA), displaying signals for intracellular trafficking and the binding of viral envelope glycoproteins, and dissociating to release its cargo to the host cell nucleus (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The Cp assembly domain (Cp149) represents the minimum protein length required to achieve self-association of dimers into archetypal capsids.
source: The Cp assembly domain (Cp149) represents the minimum protein length required to achieve self-association of dimers into archetypal capsids (Zlotnick et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zlotnick et al., 1996.

claim: Atomic models of the assembly domain capsid (4 MDa) have been determined crystallographically via symmetry averaging.
source: Atomic models of the assembly domain capsid (4 MDa) have been determined crystallographically via symmetry averaging (Wynne et al., 1999; Bourne et al., 2006; Katen et al., 2013; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple crystallographic studies.

claim: Full-length Cp includes 34 additional residues on its C-terminus (Cp183).
source: Full-length Cp includes 34 additional residues on its C-terminus (Cp183).
evidence: The claim is based on established structural knowledge of the HBV capsid protein.

claim: The C-terminal domain (CTD) tails interact with pgRNA in the immature capsid.
source: The C-terminal domain (CTD) tails interact with pgRNA in the immature capsid, extrude to the capsid exterior to signal key events during the viral life cycle, and are subject to phosphorylation and dephosphorylation (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: The CTD tails extrude to the capsid exterior to signal key events during the viral life cycle.
source: The C-terminal domain (CTD) tails interact with pgRNA in the immature capsid, extrude to the capsid exterior to signal key events during the viral life cycle, and are subject to phosphorylation and dephosphorylation (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: The CTD tails are subject to phosphorylation and dephosphorylation.
source: The C-terminal domain (CTD) tails interact with pgRNA in the immature capsid, extrude to the capsid exterior to signal key events during the viral life cycle, and are subject to phosphorylation and dephosphorylation (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016.

claim: An all-atom model of the HBV capsid assembly domain (Cp149) was constructed based on an available apo-form crystal structure (PDB ID 2G33, 3.96 Å).
source: An all-atom model of the HBV capsid assembly domain (Cp149, Figure 1a) was constructed based on an available apo-form crystal structure (PDB ID 2G33, 3.96 Å) (Bourne et al., 2006) and simulated without restraints for a total of 1.1 µs.
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling approach used in the study and is supported by citation to the crystal structure source.

claim: The HBV capsid model was simulated without restraints for a total of 1.1 µs.
source: An all-atom model of the HBV capsid assembly domain (Cp149, Figure 1a) was constructed based on an available apo-form crystal structure (PDB ID 2G33, 3.96 Å) (Bourne et al., 2006) and simulated without restraints for a total of 1.1 µs.
evidence: The claim describes the simulation timescale performed in the study.

claim: The simulation encompassed nearly 6 M atoms, including explicit water molecules and 150 mM NaCl.
source: Including explicit water molecules and 150 mM NaCl, the simulation encompassed nearly 6 M atoms.
evidence: The claim describes the system size used in the simulation.

claim: 0.1 µs of simulation time was required for the capsid to relax from its crystallographic state and reach structural equilibrium under physiological conditions.
source: Assessment of the capsid's size, stability, and morphology demonstrates that 0.1 µs of simulation time was required for the capsid to relax from its crystallographic state and reach structural equilibrium under physiological conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of simulation data regarding capsid equilibration.

claim: Capsid inner volume increased and stabilized within 0.05 µs.
source: Following the release of simulation restraints, volume increased for 0.05 µs (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: An overall expansion of capsid volume by 4% suggests that the crystal structure was substantially affected by crystal contacts.
source: An overall expansion of capsid volume by 4% suggests that the crystal structure was substantially affected by crystal contacts.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed volume expansion during simulation.

claim: Cα RMSD between capsid conformers converged to within 5 Å around 0.1 µs.
source: Cα RMSD between capsid conformers converged to within 5 Å around 0.1 µs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating the equilibration time required for the model to reach a stable configuration.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The all-atom model of the HIV-1 capsid was observed to shrink during simulation and reached equilibrium only after 0.4 µs.
source: Interestingly, the all-atom model of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) capsid (Zhao et al., 2013) was observed to shrink during simulation and reached equilibrium only after 0.4 µs (Perilla and Schulten, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous simulation studies of HIV-1 capsid.

claim: The capsid's morphology remained highly spherical throughout the course of simulation, fluctuating within 0.15% of the value calculated for the crystal structure.
source: The capsid's morphology remained highly spherical throughout the course of simulation, fluctuating within 0.15% of the value calculated for the crystal structure (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The 0.1 µs equilibration time required for the HBV capsid model is consistent with previous all-atom simulation work on the similarly sized poliovirus capsid.
source: The 0.1 µs equilibration time required for the HBV capsid model is consistent with previous all-atom simulation work on the similarly sized poliovirus capsid, which attempted to correct for anticipated volume expansion in the initial model, prior to simulation (Andoh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous simulation work on poliovirus capsid.

claim: Equilibration times are expected to be even longer for larger capsids.
source: Equilibration times are expected to be even longer for larger capsids (Perilla and Schulten, 2017) and capsids whose experimental structures were determined under conditions very different from their native environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Perilla and Schulten, 2017.

claim: Most other all-atom investigations of virus capsids have reached timescales of only tens of nanoseconds.
source: Given that most other all-atom investigations of virus capsids have reached timescales of only tens of nanoseconds, these observations underscore the likely necessity of future capsid simulation studies to sample temporal regimes of hundreds of nanoseconds in order to produce relaxed conformational ensembles conducive to the measurement of equilibrium biophysical properties.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the literature on virus capsid simulations.

claim: Future capsid simulation studies likely need to sample temporal regimes of hundreds of nanoseconds to produce relaxed conformational ensembles conducive to the measurement of equilibrium biophysical properties.
source: Given that most other all-atom investigations of virus capsids have reached timescales of only tens of nanoseconds, these observations underscore the likely necessity of future capsid simulation studies to sample temporal regimes of hundreds of nanoseconds in order to produce relaxed conformational ensembles conducive to the measurement of equilibrium biophysical properties.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the equilibration observations in this study.

claim: The HBV capsid is remarkably flexible.
source: Above all else, simulation of the HBV capsid reveals that it is remarkably flexible.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the simulation data.

claim: Local capsid dynamics arise from the internal motions of constituent Cp dimers.
source: Local capsid dynamics arise from the internal motions of constituent Cp dimers (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of simulation data and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: The flexibility of Cp is likely an essential feature, as dimers appear to be capable of a conformational switch that facilitates assembly.
source: The flexibility of Cp is likely an essential feature, as dimers appear to be capable of a conformational switch that facilitates assembly (Packianathan et al., 2010), and assembled capsids can accommodate two different T numbers (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Assembled capsids can accommodate two different T numbers.
source: The flexibility of Cp is likely an essential feature, as dimers appear to be capable of a conformational switch that facilitates assembly (Packianathan et al., 2010), and assembled capsids can accommodate two different T numbers (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The C-terminal extended structure beyond helix 5 is the most mobile segment of Cp.
source: Cα RMSF profiles indicate that the C-terminal extended structure beyond helix 5 is the most mobile segment of Cp (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSF analysis shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: RMSF values are 9.8 ± 3.1 Å at V149-Cα and 2.1 ± 0.7 Å at T142-Cα.
source: Values are 9.8 ± 3.1 Å at V149-Cα and 2.1 ± 0.7 Å at T142-Cα , the last crystallographically ordered residue in most experimental structures (Wynne et al., 1999; Bourne et al., 2006; Katen et al., 2013; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim reports specific RMSF measurements from the simulation.

claim: T142 is the last crystallographically ordered residue in most experimental structures.
source: Values are 9.8 ± 3.1 Å at V149-Cα and 2.1 ± 0.7 Å at T142-Cα , the last crystallographically ordered residue in most experimental structures (Wynne et al., 1999; Bourne et al., 2006; Katen et al., 2013; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple crystal structures.

claim: In Cp183, residues 140 to 149 have been described as a linker that connects the assembly domain to the disordered CTD.
source: In Cp183, residues 140 to 149 have been described as a linker (Watts et al., 2002) that connects the assembly domain to the disordered CTD, whose flexibility and mobility are known to be vital for capsid function throughout the infection cycle (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Watts et al., 2002 and Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The flexibility and mobility of the CTD are known to be vital for capsid function throughout the infection cycle.
source: In Cp183, residues 140 to 149 have been described as a linker (Watts et al., 2002) that connects the assembly domain to the disordered CTD, whose flexibility and mobility are known to be vital for capsid function throughout the infection cycle (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: CD dimers are more flexible than AB dimers.
source: Comparing average Cα RMSF for dimer groups indicates that CD dimers are more flexible than AB dimers (Figure 2b–c).
evidence: The claim is based on RMSF analysis shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: The spike tips at the junction of helices 3 and 4 and the region encompassing helix 2 and its connecting loop to helix 3 exhibit the greatest mobility apart from the C-termini.
source: Apart from the C-termini, the spike tips at the junction of helices 3 and 4 and the region encompassing helix 2 and its connecting loop to helix 3 exhibit the greatest mobility.
evidence: The claim is based on RMSF analysis from the simulation.

claim: The flexibility and variability of the CD dimer exceeds that of the AB dimer in the spike tips and helix 2 region.
source: The flexibility and variability of the CD dimer exceeds that of the AB dimer in both of these key locations, demonstrating that local capsid dynamics are a function of quasi-equivalence.
evidence: The claim is based on RMSF analysis from the simulation.

claim: Local capsid dynamics are a function of quasi-equivalence.
source: The flexibility and variability of the CD dimer exceeds that of the AB dimer in both of these key locations, demonstrating that local capsid dynamics are a function of quasi-equivalence.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential flexibility observed between AB and CD dimers.

claim: CD dimers exhibit more disorder in the spike tips than AB dimers in the crystal structure.
source: Even within the crystal structure, CD dimers exhibit more disorder in the spike tips than AB dimers (Bourne et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the crystal structure.

claim: CD dimer spike tips maintain a shorter gap between constituent chains than AB dimer spike tips (4.9 ± 4.4 Å versus 7.2 ± 5.2 Å from D78-Cα to D78-Cα' on average during simulation).
source: CD dimer spike tips also maintain a shorter gap between constituent chains than AB dimer spike tips (4.9 ± 4.4 Å versus 7.2 ± 5.2 Å from D78-Cα to D78-Cα' on average during simulation), indicating that greater mobility in this region does not arise from or lead to a more open dimer interface.
evidence: The claim reports specific distance measurements from the simulation.

claim: Greater mobility in the spike tip region does not arise from or lead to a more open dimer interface.
source: CD dimer spike tips also maintain a shorter gap between constituent chains than AB dimer spike tips (4.9 ± 4.4 Å versus 7.2 ± 5.2 Å from D78-Cα to D78-Cα' on average during simulation), indicating that greater mobility in this region does not arise from or lead to a more open dimer interface.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the distance measurements.

claim: Spikes composed of both AB and CD dimers demonstrate the ability to sway back and forth.
source: An interesting observation from simulation is that spikes composed of both AB and CD dimers demonstrate the ability to sway back and forth.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the simulation.

claim: The effects of quasi-equivalence on capsid dynamics could play an important, but as yet unknown role in capsid function.
source: Because the structural features of viruses have been highly optimized to carry out specific functions necessary to drive infection, it is reasonable to hypothesize that the effects of quasi-equivalence on capsid dynamics could play an important, but as yet unknown role in capsid function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed differences in dynamics.

claim: The capsid exhibits global dynamics that arise from spatial movements of dimers relative to each other within the assembly.
source: Beyond the internal motions of Cp dimers, the capsid exhibits global dynamics that arise from spatial movements of dimers relative to each other within the assembly.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of simulation data.

claim: The increase in apparent dimer flexibility when considering the full capsid context arises from spatial movements of dimers relative to each other within the capsid assembly.
source: Comparison of average Cα RMSF measured for dimers extracted from the capsid (Figure 3a, bottom curve) with that of dimers considered within the context of the capsid (Figure 3a, top curve) clearly illustrates this observation.
evidence: The claim is based on RMSF comparison shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The relative motion of dimers leads to asymmetry within the capsid structure.
source: The relative motion of dimers leads immediately to asymmetry within the capsid structure.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed dimer motions.

claim: Capsid dynamics can cause deviations in the transformations between dimers of neighboring subunits in excess of ±8°.
source: Capsid dynamics can cause deviations in the transformations between dimers of neighboring subunits in excess of ±8° (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), leading to spatial displacements of up to ±8 Å compared to a symmetric structure.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deviations in transformations between dimers lead to spatial displacements of up to ±8 Å compared to a symmetric structure.
source: Capsid dynamics can cause deviations in the transformations between dimers of neighboring subunits in excess of ±8° (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), leading to spatial displacements of up to ±8 Å compared to a symmetric structure.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Projection of capsid RMSF values onto their corresponding locations in the capsid model illustrates a clear picture of asymmetry in global dynamics.
source: Projection of capsid RMSF values onto their corresponding locations in the capsid model illustrates a clear picture of asymmetry in global dynamics (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is based on visualization shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Combining the global motions sampled over the simulation timescale of 1 μs does not yield an idealized icosahedral structure.
source: Given infinite conformational sampling (or icosahedral averaging), the projection might be expected to appear symmetric; however, combining the global motions sampled over the simulation timescale of 1 μs does not yield an idealized icosahedral structure.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the RMSF projection.

claim: Global dynamics appear non-uniform and follow no distinguishable pattern.
source: Beyond consistently high flexibility of the spikes, global dynamics appear non-uniform and follow no distinguishable pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the RMSF projection.

claim: RMSF values do not correlate with symmetry axes or correspond strongly to capsomere type.
source: RMSF values do not correlate with symmetry axes or correspond strongly to capsomere type.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the RMSF data.

claim: Hexamers are slightly more flexible than pentamers on average (6.7 ± 0.3 Å versus 6.2 ± 0.2 Å).
source: Assessment of the local stability of capsomeres based on RMSD from the initial model indicates that hemaxers are slightly more flexible than pentamers on average (6.7 ± 0.3 Å versus 6.2 ± 0.2 Å), which can be attributed to the increased flexibility measured for CD dimers.
evidence: The claim reports specific RMSD measurements from the simulation.

claim: The increased flexibility of hexamers compared to pentamers can be attributed to the increased flexibility measured for CD dimers.
source: Assessment of the local stability of capsomeres based on RMSD from the initial model indicates that hemaxers are slightly more flexible than pentamers on average (6.7 ± 0.3 Å versus 6.2 ± 0.2 Å), which can be attributed to the increased flexibility measured for CD dimers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the RMSD measurements and dimer flexibility analysis.

claim: In the HIV-1 capsid, hexamers were found to be notably more flexible than pentamers (3.8 ± 1.0 Å versus 2.7 ± 0.6 Å).
source: This is in contrast to results for the HIV-1 capsid, whose hexamers were found to be notably more flexible than pentamers (3.8 ± 1.0 Å versus 2.7 ± 0.6 Å) (Perilla and Schulten, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Perilla and Schulten, 2017.

claim: Apparent asymmetry of capsomeres within the context of the capsid assembly arises from translations through space, which do not occur uniformly and are not fully sampled across symmetrically related regions of the capsid over 1 µs.
source: Apparent asymmetry of capsomeres within the context of the capsid assembly arises from translations through space, which do not occur uniformly and are not fully sampled across symmetrically related regions of the capsid over 1 µs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the analysis of capsomere motions.

claim: The time series for spatial fluctuations of capsid pentamers with respect to the capsid center reveals correlation, anti-correlation, and lack of correlation in the motions of symmetrically related pentamers.
source: Indeed, the time series for spatial fluctuations of capsid pentamers with respect to the capsid center reveals correlation, anti-correlation, and lack of correlation in the motions of symmetrically related pentamers (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: These observations indicate asymmetric distortions in capsid shape at equilibrium, and that capsid shape constantly fluctuates over long timescales.
source: These observations indicate asymmetric distortions in capsid shape at equilibrium, and that capsid shape constantly fluctuates over long timescales.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pentamer fluctuation analysis.

claim: Normal mode analysis (NMA) has been applied to compute collective motions of icosahedral capsids.
source: In particular, normal mode analysis (NMA) has been applied to compute collective motions of icosahedral capsids, which have proven useful for suggesting pathways for large conformational transitions involving global expansion, such as swelling and maturation (Tama and Brooks, 2002; Tama and Brooks, 2005; Kim et al., 2003; Rader et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple NMA studies.

claim: NMA calculations of icosahedral capsids have relied on the use of symmetry constraints to minimize computational expense.
source: To minimize computational expense, such calculations have relied on the use of symmetry constraints.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of NMA methodology.

claim: Essential dynamics of the capsid were determined by principal component analysis (PCA) of its Cα trace, using 50,000 conformations sampled over 1 µs of simulation.
source: Essential dynamics of the capsid were determined by principal component analysis (PCA) of its Cα trace, using 50,000 conformations sampled over 1 µs of simulation.
evidence: The claim describes the PCA methodology used in the study.

claim: PCA results reveal remarkable complexity in the capsid's local and global dynamics and further emphasize asymmetric distortion in its overall shape.
source: PCA results reveal remarkable complexity in the capsid's local and global dynamics and further emphasize asymmetric distortion in its overall shape.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of PCA results.

claim: The lowest frequency mode comprises only 6% of total variance.
source: The lowest frequency mode (Figure 5) comprises only 6% of total variance; by the tenth mode, contribution to variance is less than 2% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim reports specific PCA results shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: By the tenth mode, contribution to variance is less than 2%.
source: The lowest frequency mode (Figure 5) comprises only 6% of total variance; by the tenth mode, contribution to variance is less than 2% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim reports specific PCA results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: More than 25 modes are required to account for 50% of the collective motions sampled by the capsid.
source: More than 25 modes are required to account for 50% of the collective motions sampled by the capsid.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of PCA results.

claim: Previous work to predict collective motions of the HBV capsid based on NMA with symmetry constraints reported motions such as outward expansion of Cps on fivefold vertices coupled with inward expansion of Cps on threefold vertices, capsid breathing, twisting of Cps on fivefold and threefold vertices in opposite directions, and pinching of Cps on fivefold and threefold vertices toward those vertices.
source: Previous work to predict collective motions of the HBV capsid based on NMA with symmetry constraints reported motions such as (1) an outward expansion of Cps on fivefold vertices coupled with inward expansion of Cps on threefold vertices, (2) capsid breathing, (3) twisting of Cps on fivefold and threefold vertices in opposite directions, and (4) pinching of Cps on fivefold and threefold vertices toward those vertices (Dykeman and Sankey, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dykeman and Sankey, 2010.

claim: The modes computed in the present study include no assumption of symmetry and cannot be simply described as previously reported motions.
source: The modes computed in the present study include no assumption of symmetry and cannot be so simply described, as they encompass varied combinations of previously reported motions, a well as other movements, distributed non-uniformly across the capsid structure.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of PCA results with previous NMA studies.

claim: One common characteristic observed for all major modes was an elongation or compression of the capsid along one axis or another, resulting in the protrusion of some area of its surface and, thus, asymmetric distortion of its shape.
source: One common characteristic observed for all major modes was an elongation or compression of the capsid along one axis or another, resulting in the protrusion of some area of its surface and, thus, asymmetric distortion of its shape.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of PCA modes.

claim: A symmetric breathing mode, which was previously predicted for the HBV capsid, was not identified by PCA.
source: Notably, a symmetric breathing mode, which was previously predicted for the HBV capsid (Dykeman and Sankey, 2010), was not identified by PCA.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of PCA results with previous NMA predictions.

claim: Given infinite conformational sampling, the symmetric features of the capsid's essential dynamics might be expected to appear more pronounced.
source: Given infinite conformational sampling, the symmetric features of the capsid's essential dynamics might be expected to appear more pronounced.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference about sampling limitations.

claim: Some NMA studies of icosahedral capsids have suggested that the lowest frequency modes may actually be non-icosahedral, implying that asymmetric motions could be the most relevant to biological function.
source: Importantly, some NMA studies of icosahedral capsids have suggested that the lowest frequency modes may actually be non-icosahedral, implying that asymmetric motions could be the most relevant to biological function (Tama and Brooks, 2002; Rader et al., 2005; May et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple NMA studies.

claim: More recent studies using multi-scale techniques that combine NMA with symmetry-constrained MD simulations suggest that, although asymmetric paths contribute to the ensemble of pathways available for expansion transitions, the symmetric paths dominate.
source: However, more recent studies using multi-scale techniques that combine NMA with symmetry-constrained MD simulations suggest that, although asymmetric paths contribute to the ensemble of pathways available for expansion transitions, the symmetric paths dominate (May et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to May et al., 2012.

claim: The observation that the capsid is capable of asymmetric distortion, even under equilibrium conditions and in the absence of mechanical stress, raises the possibility that this may be an important biophysical feature, relevant to capsid function.
source: Regardless of the role of symmetry in long timescale dynamics of the HBV capsid, the observation that the capsid is capable of asymmetric distortion, even under equilibrium conditions and in the absence of mechanical stress, raises the possibility that this may be an important biophysical feature, relevant to capsid function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed asymmetric distortions.

claim: The best cryo-EM resolution achieved thus far for the HBV capsid is 3.5 Å.
source: The best cryo-EM resolution achieved thus far for the HBV capsid is 3.5 Å (Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Analysis of theoretical density maps calculated for conformations sampled during simulation demonstrate that the high flexibility of the capsid is a key factor limiting the resolution obtained for it in single-particle image reconstructions.
source: Analysis of theoretical density maps calculated for conformations sampled during simulation demonstrate that the high flexibility of the capsid is a key factor limiting the resolution obtained for it in single-particle image reconstructions.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of theoretical density maps from the simulation.

claim: Density maps were calculated for 1,000 capsid conformations extracted at regular intervals over 1 µs of simulation time.
source: Density maps were calculated for 1,000 capsid conformations extracted at regular intervals over 1 µs of simulation time.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for theoretical density map calculation.

claim: The average map exhibits significant smoothing relative to the map calculated for a single conformation.
source: The average map (Figure 6b) exhibits significant smoothing relative to the map calculated for a single conformation (Figure 6a), and the loss of detail clearly stems from the collective variability of capsid conformations included in the analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of density maps shown in Figure 6a and 6b.

claim: The loss of detail in the average map clearly stems from the collective variability of capsid conformations included in the analysis.
source: The average map (Figure 6b) exhibits significant smoothing relative to the map calculated for a single conformation (Figure 6a), and the loss of detail clearly stems from the collective variability of capsid conformations included in the analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the density map analysis.

claim: Differences in pentamer-pentamer diameter between individual maps were found to exceed 4 Å.
source: Differences in pentamer-pentamer diameter between individual maps were found to exceed 4 Å, which would be more than sufficient to cause smearing in experimental density.
evidence: The claim reports specific measurements from the density map analysis.

claim: Differences in pentamer-pentamer diameter exceeding 4 Å would be more than sufficient to cause smearing in experimental density.
source: Differences in pentamer-pentamer diameter between individual maps were found to exceed 4 Å, which would be more than sufficient to cause smearing in experimental density.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the measured diameter differences.

claim: Applying icosahedral averaging results in further degradation of atomic detail.
source: Applying icosahedral averaging, as is common for structure determination of virus capsids with both cryo-EM and crystallography, results in further degradation of atomic detail (Figure 6c).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of density maps shown in Figure 6b and 6c.

claim: Given infinite conformational sampling, the maps from Figure 6b and c would likely exhibit yet less detail, but more closely resemble one another.

source: Mutations in the Cp assembly domain, distant from the packaged pgRNA, result in a capsid that supports reverse transcription of only one strand of the viral genome, suggesting that capsid dynamics play an important role in genome replication (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claim: Capsid dynamics play an important role in genome replication.
source: Mutations in the Cp assembly domain, distant from the packaged pgRNA, result in a capsid that supports reverse transcription of only one strand of the viral genome, suggesting that capsid dynamics play an important role in genome replication (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations, supported by citation.

claim: A novel treatment strategy for HBV may lie in the development of small-molecule drugs designed to increase capsid rigidity or otherwise limit the relative degrees of freedom of subunits.
source: A novel treatment strategy for HBV may, thus, lie in the development of small-molecule drugs designed to increase capsid rigidity or otherwise limit the relative degrees of freedom of subunits, such that key dynamical properties are suppressed or any necessary asymmetric distortion becomes impossible.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the importance of capsid dynamics.

claim: Recent work has shown that a class of HBV capsid-directed antiviral compounds not only modulate assembly, but also cause pre-formed capsids to become asymmetric.
source: Recent work has shown that a class of HBV capsid-directed antiviral compounds not only modulate assembly, but also cause pre-formed capsids to become asymmetric (Perilla et al., 2016; Schlicksup et al., 2018), underscoring the ability of drugs to alter capsid structure and further demonstrating the capsid's readiness to undergo distortion in response to external stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Perilla et al., 2016 and Schlicksup et al., 2018.

claim: Mechanical malleability of the HBV capsid has been attributed to relatively loose packing of its constituent Cp dimers compared to packing of other capsids.
source: Mechanical malleability of the HBV capsid has been attributed to relatively loose packing of its constituent Cp dimers compared to packing of other capsids (Arkhipov et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Arkhipov et al., 2009.

claim: The complex dynamics observed during simulation may result from loose subunit packing, relatively weak interaction energies between capsid subunits, and/or a relatively flat energy surface for different inter-subunit interactions.
source: The complex dynamics observed during simulation, as well as variability in collective motions across the capsid within single modes, may result from such loose subunit packing, relatively weak interaction energies between capsid subunits (Ceres and Zlotnick, 2002), and/or a relatively flat energy surface for different inter-subunit interactions, all of which can contribute to global flexibility and, thus, asymmetry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation observations and previous work, with citation.

claim: Structural diversity arising from capsid flexibility and asymmetry is likely critical to viral function.
source: Moreover, structural diversity arising from capsid flexibility and asymmetry is likely critical to viral function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed flexibility and asymmetry.

claim: Conformational variations contribute to entropic stabilization of the capsid, which may be an important component of the hysteresis between assembly and disassembly reactions.
source: Conformational variations contribute to entropic stabilization of the capsid, which may be an important component of the hysteresis between assembly and disassembly reactions.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the conformational diversity.

claim: Entropic mechanisms are now known to play an important role in allosteric regulation and protein-protein interaction.
source: Entropic mechanisms are now known to play an important role in allosteric regulation and protein-protein interaction (Hilser et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hilser et al., 2012.

claim: Asymmetry in virus particles can be defined in terms of a distinct structural feature, structural defects, or stochastic dynamical effects.
source: From a cryo-EM perspective, asymmetry in virus particles can be defined in terms of a distinct structural feature (such as a bound receptor), structural defects, or stochastic dynamical effects (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: There have been asymmetric reconstructions of HBV containing pgRNA and reverse transcriptase.
source: There have been a number of asymmetric reconstructions of icosahedral viruses that treat asymmetry with respect to a structural feature, including HBV containing pgRNA and reverse transcriptase (Wang et al., 2014), canine parvovirus bound to a single receptor (Hafenstein et al., 2007), MS2 bound to a pilus (Dent et al., 2013), and MS2 with genome (Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Asymmetry with respect to particle defects was explored in a recent analysis of Ross River virus.
source: Asymmetry with respect to particle defects was explored in a recent analysis of Ross River virus (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: The present work has enabled investigation of the effects of asymmetry driven by protein dynamics.
source: The present work has enabled investigation of the effects of asymmetry driven by protein dynamics.
evidence: The claim is based on the unique contribution of this simulation study.

claim: Capsid flexibility and asymmetry were sufficient to cause notable blurring of the final averaged density map, particularly when icosahedral averaging was applied.
source: Despite the all-atom level of detail encompassed by simulation, capsid flexibility and asymmetry were sufficient to cause notable blurring of the final map, particularly when icosahedral averaging was applied.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of theoretical density maps.

claim: In the absence of experimental error, simulation results indicate that thermal motion of particles makes large contributions to limiting the resolution of image reconstructions.
source: Yet, in the absence of experimental error, simulation results indicate that thermal motion of particles makes large contributions to limiting the resolution of image reconstructions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the theoretical resolution analysis.

claim: New 3D classification techniques can separate substantially different states, but the structural variation and diversity observed during simulation suggests a continuum of states, which will be difficult for image processing software to distinguish.
source: New 3D classification techniques can separate substantially different states, but the structural variation and diversity observed during simulation suggests a continuum of states, which will be difficult for image processing software to distinguish.

claim: Capsid dynamics may lead to a large fraction of images being discarded due to particle heterogeneity.
source: Capsid dynamics may also lead to a large fraction of images being discarded due to particle heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the capsid flexibility.

claim: Even in this era of increasing cryo-EM resolution, intrinsic capsid flexibility may represent a major limiting factor to achieving true atomic (1–2 Å) resolution.
source: Thus, even in this era of increasing cryo-EM resolution, intrinsic capsid flexibility may represent a major limiting factor to achieving true atomic (1–2 Å) resolution.

claim: Symmetry relaxation methods may warrant greater consideration in future work.
source: Symmetry relaxation methods may warrant greater consideration in future work.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the findings of asymmetry.

claim: The ability of the capsid to differentiate ionic species and preferentially translocate those that are positively charged may play a role in facilitating the extrusion of the positively charged CTD tails through the capsid's pores to expose them to the surface for cellular signaling.
source: The ability of the capsid to differentiate ionic species and preferentially translocate those that are positively charged may play a role in facilitating the extrusion of the positively charged CTD tails through the capsid's pores to expose them to the surface for cellular signaling.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the ion exchange preferences.

claim: By the same logic, the addition of negative charges on the CTD tails by phosphorylation could serve to slow the rate of extrusion.
source: By the same logic, the addition of negative charges on the CTD tails by phosphorylation could serve to slow the rate of extrusion, accounting in part for the observation that Cp183 phosphorylation-mimic mutants show reduced rates of proteolytic cleavage, consistent with reduced exposure to the capsid exterior (Selzer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the ion exchange preferences and experimental observations, with citation.

claim: Based on its ion exchange preferences, the capsid could employ phosphorylation and dephosphorylation to modulate its own cellular signaling process.
source: Thus, based on its ion exchange preferences, the capsid could employ phosphorylation and dephosphorylation to modulate its own cellular signaling process.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the ion exchange analysis.

claim: Ion occupancy maps indicate that the translocation of sodium ions primarily occurs through the triangular pores located on either side of CD dimers, suggesting that these apertures may also represent the gateways of CTD tail extrusion.
source: Ion occupancy maps indicate that the translocation of sodium ions primarily occurs through the triangular pores located on either side of CD dimers, suggesting that these apertures may also represent the gateways of CTD tail extrusion.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the ion occupancy analysis.

claim: Cryo-EM studies have implicated the capsid hexamers as the sites of extrusion based on structural observation of a protein kinase within the hexameric valleys of the capsid exterior, presumably bound there to CTD tails.
source: Cryo-EM studies have implicated the capsid hexamers as the sites of extrusion based on structural observation of a protein kinase within the hexameric valleys of the capsid exterior, presumably bound there to CTD tails (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Hexameric valleys are each surrounded by six triangular pores, and as the largest valleys between capsid spikes, they may represent the most accessible location along the surface for close approach of a kinase for CTD tail binding.
source: Hexameric valleys are each surrounded by six triangular pores, and as the largest valleys between capsid spikes, they may represent the most accessible location along the surface for close approach of a kinase for CTD tail binding.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural analysis.

claim: The triangular pores are the largest surface apertures, and are, thus, best able to accommodate translocation of the peptide chains that comprise CTD tails.
source: Further, the triangular pores are the largest surface apertures, and are, thus, best able to accommodate translocation of the peptide chains that comprise CTD tails.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural analysis.

claim: The swaying motion of capsid spikes identified by simulation could function to guide CTD tails extruded through triangular pores to their neighboring hexameric valleys for interaction with kinases for phosphorylation.
source: The swaying motion of capsid spikes identified by simulation could function to guide CTD tails extruded through triangular pores to their neighboring hexameric valleys for interaction with kinases for phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the spike dynamics.

claim: Enhanced flexibility of CD dimer spikes relative to AB dimer spikes could bias the movement of CTD tails to hexameric valleys rather than pentameric valleys.
source: Enhanced flexibility of CD dimer spikes relative to AB dimer spikes could bias the movement of CTD tails to hexameric valleys rather than pentameric valleys, which may be too spatially restrictive to accommodate kinase approach.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the differential spike flexibility.

claim: If the capsid's triangular pores are indeed the location of CTD extrusion and therefore play a critical role in cellular signaling, a novel treatment strategy for HBV may lie in the development of a peptide designed to block the pore to prevent extrusion and inhibit signaling.
source: If the capsid's triangular pores are indeed the location of CTD extrusion and therefore play a critical role in cellular signaling, a novel treatment strategy for HBV may lie in the development of a peptide designed to block the pore to prevent extrusion and inhibit signaling.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the proposed role of triangular pores.

claim: Recent work on the HIV-1 capsid demonstrated the tractability of pores as drug targets, describing a channel inhibitor that blocks the pores to prevent nucleotide translocation into the capsid and, thereby, suppresses reverse transcription.
source: Recent work on the HIV-1 capsid demonstrated the tractability of pores as drug targets, describing a channel inhibitor that blocks the pores to prevent nucleotide translocation into the capsid and, thereby, suppresses reverse transcription (Jacques et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jacques et al., 2016.

claim: Pore-blocking drugs could also serve to inhibit reverse transcription in the HBV capsid.
source: Pore-blocking drugs could also serve to inhibit reverse transcription in the HBV capsid.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the HIV-1 example.

claim: Strong localization of sodium ions observed within the capsid's triangular pores appears to enhance dimer-dimer interaction in regions of high negative charge.
source: Strong localization of sodium ions observed within the capsid's triangular pores appears to enhance dimer-dimer interaction in regions of high negative charge.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ion occupancy analysis.

claim: Positively charged metal ions have been shown experimentally to increase the rate of capsid assembly.
source: Positively charged metal ions have been shown experimentally to increase the rate of capsid assembly (Ceres and Zlotnick, 2002; Stray et al., 2004; Choi et al., 2005), possibly through specific binding to Cp (Ceres and Zlotnick, 2002; Stray et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies.

claim: Zinc and nickel have been shown to accelerate assembly at much lower concentrations than monovalent cations and are hypothesized to function by binding Cp dimers and inducing them to adopt an assembly active conformation.
source: Zinc and nickel have been shown to accelerate assembly at much lower concentrations than monovalent cations and are hypothesized to function by binding Cp dimers and inducing them to adopt an assembly active conformation; a putative binding site for zinc ions has been proposed (Stray et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stray et al., 2004.

claim: Simulation does not identify sodium localization within the zinc binding site.
source: However, simulation does not identify sodium localization within the zinc binding site.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ion occupancy maps from the simulation.

claim: Zinc and nickel are transition metals capable of forming coordination spheres, while sodium is an alkali metal whose ionic interactions are governed primarily by electrostatics.
source: Importantly, zinc and nickel are transition metals capable of forming coordination spheres, while sodium is an alkali metal whose ionic interactions are governed primarily by electrostatics.
evidence: The claim is based on established chemical knowledge.

claim: The mechanism by which zinc and nickel accelerate assembly acts in addition to that of sodium or other non-transition metals.
source: As kinetic enhancement by divalent transition metals is conferred at lower concentrations than other divalent ions that lack coordination ability, such as calcium and magnesium (Stray et al., 2004), it is likely that the mechanism by which zinc and nickel accelerate assembly acts in addition to that of sodium or other non-transition metals.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and chemical properties, with citation.

claim: Simulation results suggest that sodium reduces electrostatic repulsion within the triangular pores where three dimers pack together to form a trimer of dimers.
source: Simulation results suggest that sodium reduces electrostatic repulsion within the triangular pores where three dimers pack together to form a trimer of dimers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ion occupancy analysis.

claim: A trimer of dimers is implicated as the nucleation core for HBV capsid assembly.
source: Importantly, a trimer of dimers is implicated as the nucleation core for HBV capsid assembly (Zlotnick et al., 1999), and electrostatic stabilization of this critical substructure may represent a mechanism by which positively charged metal ions enhance assembly kinetics.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zlotnick et al., 1999.

claim: Electrostatic stabilization of the trimer of dimers may represent a mechanism by which positively charged metal ions enhance assembly kinetics.
source: Importantly, a trimer of dimers is implicated as the nucleation core for HBV capsid assembly (Zlotnick et al., 1999), and electrostatic stabilization of this critical substructure may represent a mechanism by which positively charged metal ions enhance assembly kinetics.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the sodium localization and assembly nucleation, with citation.

claim: Such an effect is consistent with calculations suggesting that ionic strength promotes HBV capsid assembly by globally screening electrostatic repulsion between dimers.
source: Such an effect is consistent with calculations suggesting that ionic strength promotes HBV capsid assembly by globally screening electrostatic repulsion between dimers (Kegel and Schoot Pv, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kegel and Schoot Pv, 2004.

claim: Sodium binding was also observed within a trimeric dimer interface in the HIV-1 capsid.
source: Interestingly, sodium binding was also observed within a trimeric dimer interface in the HIV-1 capsid (Perilla and Schulten, 2017), whose assembly is likewise thought to be nucleated by a trimer of dimers (Grime and Voth, 2012; Tsiang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Perilla and Schulten, 2017.

source: Interestingly, sodium binding was also observed within a trimeric dimer interface in the HIV-1 capsid (Perilla and Schulten, 2017), whose assembly is likewise thought to be nucleated by a trimer of dimers (Grime and Voth, 2012; Tsiang et al., 2012).
